questions.question: Explain what sustainable fishing means and the scientific ideas behind it.
questions.expected_answer: Sustainable use: meet present needs without compromising future (Brundtland 1987); use renewable resources no faster than replaced. Sustainable fishery: healthy stock with enough breeders, limited ecosystem damage, good science-based enforced management; social side: jobs, fair rights for small-scale fishers. Maximum sustainable yield; uncertainty and natural variability; precautionary principle with safety margin.

questions.question: Describe how governments manage fisheries, using the South African hake fishery as an example.
questions.expected_answer: Stock assessments (catch data, surveys, models; DFFE); Marine Living Resources Act 1998. Total allowable catch, effort limits, rights/quotas; closed seasons, closed nursery areas, size limits, bag limits, gear and mesh restrictions; enforcement: inspectors, patrol vessels, observers, satellite tracking; costly, needs cooperation. Hake: foreign fleets 1960s-70s, 200 nm zone 1977, strict science-based TACs, recovery, MSC certification 2004 (first hake fishery).

questions.question: Explain how marine protected areas, better methods, aquaculture, consumers and communities contribute to sustainable fishing.
questions.expected_answer: MPAs/no-take zones: bigger, more fish, spillover, habitat protection, research, tourism; SA 20 new MPAs in 2019, total 41, about 5% of mainland ocean; Tsitsikamma 1964. Better methods: hooks/traps, turtle excluder devices, tori lines, night setting, weighted lines, marked gear. Aquaculture: about half of seafood, abalone, mussels, oysters (Saldanha); risks: fish meal feed, pollution, disease, mangrove clearing. Consumers: SASSI 2004 (green, orange, red), app/SMS, retailer commitments; MSC and ASC ecolabels. Communities: traditional management, secure rights; Small-Scale Fisheries Policy 2012, collective rights. International: RFMOs, High Seas Treaty 2023.
